item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
If you want to know where all the tokens will get consumed in the future, here it is. Agent swarms will have massive implications in a number of enterprise domains like software development, cyber, life sciences research, AI research, finance, and more.
The ability to parallelize agents against a unified goal where the volume of work is large, or where the search space not entirely known upfront, is going to be massive.
Agents can fan out and coordinate work together on a specific mission in completely different ways from what humans are able to do. Today even in the most resource-abundant organizations, your ability to parallelize work on most projects is quite limited. Humans run into constraints on being able to communicate with one another, share status, deal with conflicts in work, keep shared context, and so on.
As AI models can handle larger context without getting confused, and as they’re able to communicate effectively across their work with shared infrastructure, they can avoid many of the pitfalls that people have.
You can see how this can lead to not just faster execution of tasks, but qualitatively different outcomes in medicine, research or defending against cyber attacks, scientific and math discoveries, and so on. This is why we’re going to need 1,000X more compute.

item.description:
作者：Nikunj Kothari 账号：@nikunj 简介：partner @fpvventures - investing in seed/A. previous: early hire @meter, @opendoor, @atlassian & others. love @shimoleejhaveri + 👦👧
Ignoring the actors in the latest debacle of VC, “philosophically” you can’t have both..
> ask a fund to show conviction, and ask to double down especially when the chips are down.
> ask them not do contracted pro rata just because it’s convenient to you from a dilution perspective or the lead fund that’s trying to get their ownership targets.
Every VC should earn the right to the cap table at every stage. But, this industry runs on contracts and handshakes, and when you break those for short term gain that erodes the already brittle trust.
For founders, another reminder to choose your partners AND contracts well. It’s so so so important. Get a good independent lawyer who will spell this out for you.
(This is so timely since just yesterday I was helping my cousin negotiate his preseed term sheet who literally wanted an arm and leg instead of a simple SAFE)

item.description:
作者：Madhu Guru 账号：@realmadhuguru 简介：Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.
Agent capabilities will soon evolve at RSI pace. Agentic security (identity, permissions, observability) will need to outpace this.
The evolutionary direction of the broader agents space is capability -> trust -> autonomy
The first phase has been about capability - can the combination of model + harness + tools + context reliably get work done?
Capabilities have gotten pretty far, so the focus now shifts to trust…does the harness / system take the right action with right permissions? Can we observe it, audit it and establish accountability?
A lot of serious work has already gone into these problems over the last couple of years.
Now the challenge gets more important. and harder.

As agents begin to do vastly more task execution in the organization than humans, our need to secure, govern, control, and audit that work will become paramount. You’ll have agents operat...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Good post to start thinking through the long term safety approaches to managing intelligence in an enterprise. As agents begin to do vastly more task execution in the organization than humans, our need to secure, govern, control, and audit that work will become paramount.
You’ll have agents operating against most of your most valuable data; they’ll be making decisions that will be harder and harder to reverse engineer; we’ll need to understand the liability and accountability regimes when models make decisions for us; and we need ways of containing the blast radius of accidentally or intentionally malicious agents.
“Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system. Not because they are necessarily malicious, but because any sufficiently capable actor with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised, and the architecture of containment and control must account for that”
In a sense, AI will need to have its “zero trust” era that security saw. And all of this leads to needing various layers of protection and auditability of what agents are doing, what data they can work with, and controls for when things go wrong. And a huge opportunity right now for those building such systems across the enterprise.

item.title: AI Models Are Now Hiding Their Cheating | Eric Ho (Goodfire)
item.description:
播客：The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:20 A lot of people who aren't in the AI field are very surprised to realize that even the, you know, smartest researchers and scientists at the frontier don't understand their creations. It's like, oh, I thought we had a handle on all of this. You know? What's going on here? The existing alignment techniques are not going to scale to superintelligence.
Speaker 1 | 00:21 - 00:34 I don't think that the... We have the recipe where we are going to be able to fully trust smarter than human intelligences. And I think this is a consensus opinion at all of the the Frontier Labs.
Speaker 2 | 00:34 - 01:00 Hi. I'm Matt Turk. Welcome back to the MAD podcast. My guest today is Eric Ho, CEO of Good With every top AI lab now reporting agents going rogue and hacking external systems, something is clearly broken in the world of AI safety. This may be a major moment for interpretability, which is the science of looking inside the model and Eric's team to show that you can catch a model in the act of cheating before it even acts.
Speaker 2 | 01:00 - 01:35 Please enjoy my conversation with Eric from Goodfire. I want to start with this super interesting paper that the Goodfire team just published just last week, just a few days ago, entitled Models Know When They Are Reward Hacking and we can catch them at scale. And the paper opens up with the, hugging face hack and then, starts with a sentence I I really loved, where you guys say AI agents are like amoral students with a mostly absent teacher. What do you mean by that?
Speaker 1 | 01:35 - 02:05 I think we mean that AI agents really don't have human morals or values encoded into them like we would really want, I guess. And so, the the teacher that we typically have right now is some combination of pre training, but mostly RL. RL is the teacher. We give agents these rewards and penalize them if they don't get an answer correctly. And this is how they learn about the world and how to act and how to take take actions.
Speaker 1 | 02:06 - 02:48 And so we have a mostly absent teacher in terms of morality. You only have a teacher that gives you reward if you get the answer correct and a penalty if you get the answer wrong. And so it doesn't really have anything to do with morality or values. It's just, did you get this math problem correct or not? And, I think that, especially when you kind of see the future of AI agents really taking a lot more action out in the real world, means that we have these really amoral, very, very capable models running around and potentially doing things that we humans would consider, morally, you know, wrong.
Speaker 2 | 02:49 - 02:57 That brings us to the concept of reward hacking that we should, define at the very beginning of this conversation. So what's the short version of what reward hacking means?
Speaker 1 | 02:57 - 03:38 Reward hacking is a little bit tough to to pin down in terms of, like, the the precise definition, but we conceptualize it as the model kind of chasing reward and doing something that it wasn't really supposed to do when it... In in the pursuit of chasing some tore... Some form of a goal. And you can call it kind of also a goal misgeneralization where it's not really understanding what you actually intended to, specify when it's pursuing its reward. But, you know, the classic example of reward hacking is like, let's say you're training some type of video game avatar to, like, via via reinforcement learning.
Speaker 1 | 03:39 - 03:58 And then you see kind of your avatar, like, spinning around in the corner because there's a bug in your code, but it, like, makes the number go up and the the reward go up. And so that's kind of my mental image whenever I think of reward hacking. It's just like this little avatar spinning around in the corner, getting a bunch of reward, but not really doing anything productive.
Speaker 2 | 03:58 - 04:12 Or, another one I heard, and, let let me know if that feels right, is, this idea that the model is like a student that, instead of, like, working for the exam would realize it's actually much easier and faster just to steal the answer key to the exam.
Speaker 1 | 04:12 - 04:45 100%. Yeah. So I think the most salient examples of reward hacking right now are, well, of course, like the hugging face incident, but then also just, when you take a look at all these AI agents in evaluation scenarios, like SWE bench or, like, all of the common evals, all these agents reward hack incessantly. So, like, Kimi k three, I think, reward hacks on 96% of SWE bench. And so it basically does anything it possibly can to cheat on the exam rather than to actually solve the the problem.
Speaker 1 | 04:45 - 04:57 So it'll try to recall the answer. It'll try to look it up. It'll try to comb through logs and look at, like, the commit history of these repos in order to just, like, try to cheat on the the exam, basically.
Speaker 2 | 04:58 - 05:16 So you guys tested, three leading open source models. The key takeaway was that, reward hacking is pervasive, right? Like all of them do it and you just mentioned that 96 numbers. So which, were those models And, just unpack the the the number for us.
Speaker 1 | 05:16 - 05:40 Yeah. So it's three models, Kimi k three, GLM 5.2, and Quen 3.8. And really, like, they all reward hack incessantly. They just, try to do anything, that it possibly takes in order to not actually solve the problem, but, just kind of, like, cheat on, cheat on the exam, basically. So they'll try to recall the answer.
Speaker 1 | 05:40 - 06:08 They'll try to look it up. They'll try to... And, I mean, in the extreme scenarios, like in the hugging face incident, they'll try to hack their way into into something in order to look up the answers or gain some type of advantage in solving their problem. And so we were really trying to investigate this behavior, and we were actually working on this, you know, prior to the Hugging Face incident. But we were trying to investigate this behavior that we knew would be a really big, big deal.
Speaker 2 | 06:08 - 06:15 And when you guys say that, the models know that they are reward hacking, what does that mean?
Speaker 1 | 06:15 - 07:12 You know, this gets into theory of mind a little bit, which, you know, the the word know is a little imprecise. But what we mean by the word know is, there's something in their activations, essentially, the the neurons that get activated during a forward pass of the model when the model is producing a token, that encode the concept of cheating or reward hacking. And we're able to verify this both causally by kind of perturbing this idea of cheating and understanding kind of what that does to the downstream generation that the model gives, as well as really being able to verify this by a external judge. So an external judge will see, hey, whether the model actually reward hacked or not. And you can kind of verify that the internal detector matches up with with that judge.
Speaker 1 | 07:13 - 07:39 And so maybe even zooming out a little bit, like, these models have just very, very rich understandings of the world and they... That's all encoded in their neural active... Activations and their neural activity as they're producing, you know, a single token. And so all of this richness, all of this understanding currently just gets, you know, thrown away. It's like all of this computation.
Speaker 1 | 07:40 - 08:10 But we can actually reverse engineer and extract and understand kind of what all of these activations mean and do. And, you know, ultimately, like, I think this is really what what we care care a lot about. And so it was actually pretty surprising that we're able to find this, like, very robust concept of cheating, in all of these these models, the the the way that we did. But these models just really know that they're cheating when they're actually taking these these cheating actions.
Speaker 2 | 08:10 - 08:45 Great. And we'll how this all ...
